Empirical Research Plan: “Does Just Crossing the 1,500-Gram Line Save Infants?”

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Sharp (or very nearly sharp) Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) at the 1,500-gram threshold.

Why RDD fits:
• The treatment—being classified as VLBW and thereby triggering additional neonatal resources—is assigned deterministically by a one-dimensional, continuously measured running variable (birth weight).  
• Infants just above and just below 1,500 g are physiologically almost identical; any discontinuous jump in mortality can therefore be attributed to the change in medical treatment intensity, not underlying health.  
• The birth-weight distribution is extremely dense around 1,500 g, giving a large sample for precise local estimates.  
• The institutional rule is stable over time, so we do not need difference-in-differences or panel variation.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable:  Dᵢ = 1{birth weight < 1,500 g}. Interpreted as receiving the VLBW classification and associated care bundle.

Control group: Infants with birth weights just above the cutoff (e.g., 1,500–2,000 g, but identification will rely on a narrow optimal bandwidth, typically ±125 g or so).

Treatment timing: Immediate (at birth).

Running variable and cutoff:  
• Xᵢ = birth weight in grams (measured to the nearest gram).  
• Cutoff c = 1,500 g.  
We will also run a “donut” RD that excludes observations in [1,495 g, 1,505 g] to mitigate mechanical heaping right at 1,500 g.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in X at c. Mortality risk would evolve smoothly in the absence of differential treatment; any jump is due to VLBW classification. Plausibility: There is no known biological breakpoint exactly at 1,500 g.

A2. No precise manipulation of X around c. Parents and physicians cannot target a specific in utero weight on the gram; birth weight is realized after delivery. Plausibility: Very high, but rounding/heaping must be checked.

A3. Accurate measurement of X with minimal classical error. Birth weight is measured on calibrated scales immediately after birth; error variance at the ±50 g level is small relative to bandwidths. Plausibility: Good, but heaping at multiples of 50 g warrants robustness checks.

A4. Treatment status is a deterministic step function of X (sharp RD). In practice it is very close: neonatal protocols use <1,500 g as the gatekeeper. If compliance is imperfect (e.g., some >1,500 g infants receive VLBW care), we can implement fuzzy RD using first-stage discontinuity.

A5. Local independence of covariates. Non-weight covariates (gender, maternal age, race, gestational age) should evolve smoothly across the cutoff. Plausibility: Can be tested directly.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation

T1. Heaping / rounding at 1,500 g (density discontinuity).  
Mitigation: Conduct McCrary (2008) density test; implement donut RD and/or reseat running variable to 50-g bins; run robustness with measurement-error-robust bias-correction (BAK 2020).

T2. Birth weight itself strongly predicts mortality (slope).  
Mitigation: Use local linear RD with separate slopes on either side; small bandwidth (data-driven MSE-optimal from Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik); robust bias-corrected confidence intervals.

T3. Other protocols keyed to additional thresholds (e.g., 1,000 g).  
Mitigation: Restrict sample to ±300 g window around 1,500 g to avoid spillovers; placebo tests at pseudo-cutoffs (e.g., 1,300 g, 1,700 g) where no classification changes.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline

```r
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # for general regressions
library(rdrobust)    # primary RD estimation
library(rddensity)   # McCrary test

# 1. Data loading
births <- read_csv("nvs_birth_data.csv")  # assume file name

# 2. Variable construction
births <- births %>%
  mutate(bw = birth_weight_grams,
         treat = if_else(bw < 1500, 1, 0),
         y = infant_mortality_1yr,              # 1=death within 365 days
         running = bw - 1500,                   # center at cutoff
         # example demographics for covariate balance checks
         male = (sex == "M"),
         gest_weeks = gestational_age_weeks)

# 3. Main sharp RD (local linear, bias-corrected)
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = births$y,
                    x = births$running,
                    c = 0,
                    p = 1,           # local linear
                    kernel = "triangular")

summary(rd_main)

# 4. Donut RD: drop ±5g
births_donut <- births %>%
  filter(abs(running) > 5)

rd_donut <- rdrobust(y = births_donut$y,
                     x = births_donut$running,
                     c = 0,
                     p = 1)

# 5. Density test (sorting)
rddensity_result <- rddensity(X = births$running, c = 0)
summary(rddensity_result)

# 6. Covariate continuity check (e.g., gestational weeks)
rd_cov <- rdrobust(y = births$gest_weeks,
                   x = births$running,
                   c = 0)
summary(rd_cov)

# 7. Plot RD graph
rdplot(y = births$y, x = births$running,
       c = 0, p = 1, binselect = "esmv", title = "Infant mortality around 1,500g")

# 8. OPTIONAL fuzzy RD if compliance <100%
# First stage: jump in actual care intensity (e.g., NICU_minutes)
# second stage: 2SLS within rdrobust::rdrobust or with fixest::feols + iv
```

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Prior: Crossing below 1,500 g should reduce one-year infant mortality due to more aggressive medical treatment and resource allocation. Magnitude: For infants within ±150 g of the cutoff, baseline mortality ~6–8 %. I expect a discrete drop of about 2 pp (i.e., from 7 % to 5 %), implying a 25–30 % relative reduction.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)

C1: No manipulation of running variable (density test) … 1  
C2: Covariates smooth at cutoff … 1  
C3: Correct functional form and bandwidth (robust bias-corrected local linear) … 1  
C4: Outcome not affected by other simultaneously crossing thresholds … 0.5  
C5: Robustness & placebo tests implemented … 1  

Total ≈ 4.5 / 5 — high internal validity conditional on tests passing.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages a clean institutional rule to obtain credible causal estimates of how VLBW classification alters infant mortality and thereby informs optimal neonatal resource allocation.
